proxy_language: Proto-Tupi-Guarani (Tupian family) with Classical Tupinamba (Old Tupi) as the attested anchor
proxy_rationale: 'River-and-Forest Court' is a fictional later court in Amazonia/Caribbean/northern South America with no single historical language. The best-documented Amazonian-Caribbean-coast language with a 16th-17th c. grammar and dictionary is Old Tupi (Tupinamba; Anchieta 1595, Figueira 1621, Lemos Barbosa 1951), a Tupi-Guarani language whose speakers lived along rivers and forests and whose river/forest vocabulary is rich (y 'water/river', ka'a 'forest', ibira 'tree'). Proto-Tupi-Guarani reconstructions (Jensen, Rodrigues) give a time-depth anchor. The link to a hypothetical 'court' is weak; Carib (e.g. Kari'nja/Galibi) and Arawak (Lokono/Taino) are neighboring alternatives, but Old Tupi is much better documented and gives a coherent, specialist-checkable system.
phonology: Old Tupi (Navarro/Rodrigues-style analysis). Oral vowels: a e i o u and y (high central unrounded, written y). Nasal vowels (a~ e~ i~ y~ o~ u~) are written with tilde or marked in transliteration but can be omitted in plain Latin text. Consonants: stops p t k and labiovelar kw (written kw or ku), glottal stop ' (written '), nasals m n, ng (velar nasal, 'ng'), fricatives s (also written c/z historically), x (palatal fricative, 'x' in Jesuit orthography), h in some sources; liquid r (flap); semivowels w and y~j. Voiced stops b, d, g appear as allophones of nasal+stop or in loans, but b occurs in native words from earlier *mb (e.g., ibira 'tree', abá 'man'). Stress usually on the final syllable (oxytone) or on the stressed syllable of a morphologically fixed shape; in Latin-script naming, stress is not marked.
phonotactics: Syllable structure is (C)V(C) in the classical analysis, but native words are overwhelmingly (C)V open syllables; coda consonants are rare and, where they occur, are restricted (typically a glottal stop ' or a nasal/n or a stop in older stems). Consonant clusters are absent word-internally except across morpheme boundaries and the labiovelar kw / nasal-stop sequences (mb, nd, ng as unit consonants). Words begin with a consonant or a vowel; hiatus (adjacent vowels) is tolerated and the glottal stop is often inserted between vowels (ka'a, pe'a). Words end in a vowel or a nasal; native words do not end in b, d, g, or voiced fricatives. No word-initial rr. y and i alternate; the high central y is common word-internally.
orthography: Use the standard Jesuit-based scholarly transliteration of Old Tupi as in Navarro's Dicionario de tupi antigo (2013): vowels a e i o u y; consonants p t k s x r m n ng w j (or y as glide); glottal stop as apostrophe '; kw for labiovelar. Nasal vowels may be written with tilde (a~ -> ã) but for game names a plain unmarked form is acceptable. Avoid letters c, q, f, l, v, z, d, g (alone), b (alone) in native-looking names; the unit ng, mb, nd may be used as in historical sources but are not required.
morphology: Agglutinating with a strong head-final tendency in nominal compounds and prefixed possession. Nouns are largely uninflected for case or plural; plural is optional and expressed with -etá 'many/all' or -(a)ra as collective. Possession is by prefix: a- 1sg, e- 2sg, o- 3, and a relational prefix r-/s-/t-/h- alternates with the stem (the 'relational morpheme' system: ro-, so-, t-, h-). Nominalizers: -ara/-sara 'agent, one who' (e.g. apyaba -> apyaba-ra), -aba 'instrument, place, thing' (e.g., ka'a 'forest' -> -aba), -pyra 'patient/result of' (cf. -pyra in iapyra), -ana/-rana 'like, false, ersatz', -eté 'true, real, genuine', -ussu/-guasu 'big', -mirim 'small', -ete 'true'. Verbs show person prefixes; deverbal nouns take -aba (instrument/place), -sara (agent), -pyra (product).
compounding: Noun-noun compounds and noun + attributive suffix patterns are the main device for naming. A possessor/modifier precedes the head in genitive constructions ('X's Y' = X + Y, e.g., ybytyra 'mountain'). For 'Y of X', place the modifier first: y 'water' + ka'a 'forest' etc. Descriptive adjectives follow the noun with an attributive suffix: noun + -ussu 'big', noun + -mirim 'small', noun + -eté 'true/real', noun + -rana 'false/like'. Place names commonly use '-ty/-tyba/-tiba' 'abundance of' and '-ba' 'place' (e.g., -tyba 'place abounding in': ibira + -tyba, Ubatuba from ybá-tyba?). 'Y-maker/maker of' = Y + -sara/-ara or 'verb root + -sara'. Locatives are formed with -pe 'in/at', -rupi 'through/along', -su 'toward' postposed to the noun.
noun_phrase_order: Head-final for compounds, but with attributive suffixes/adjectives after the noun: N-ADJ (e.g., yara-ussu 'big lord'). Genitive precedes head: POSSESSOR-POSSESSED. Postpositions follow the noun (N-pe 'in N', N-rupi 'along N'). Demonstratives (nde, ko, a'e, ae) precede or follow loosely; for naming, use N + modifier suffix patterns and avoid free demonstratives.

worked_examples.name: Tatá-sara
worked_examples.gloss: tatá 'fire' + -sara 'agent, one who' (cf. Old Tupi agentive -sara; shape is a pattern, not an attested lexeme)

notes: Proxy is a pragmatic choice: Old Tupi is a real, well-documented Tupi-Guarani language of river/forest peoples, used as a stand-in for an unattested 'River-and-Forest Court'; Carib and Arawak names would be equally defensible and the current game strings (Budroho, Mupiwik, etc.) do not fit Tupi-Guarani phonotactics well (voiced b/d, x, final consonants, no vowels like y). Guidelines: favor open CV syllables, vowels a e i o u y, glottal stop between vowels (ka'a), and end names in a vowel or nasal. The allowed-grapheme list includes b/d/g only for sequences like mb/nd/ng and for older loans; the audit regex forbids bare b/d/g not followed by a vowel. Avoid l, f, v, z, c, q, and word-final stops. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since the language is not Goidelic.
